beats.text: Go and get your electric bill. Right now, before we start, not the envelope, the bill.
Now don't look at what you owe. Everybody looks at what you owe.
Turn it over, second page usually, that column of small gray print where they take the bill apart.
Look at how many lines are on that cage.
You saw $214 and figured you ran the air too hard in July.
That wasn't it, neighbor. Somewhere between $30 and $60 of what's on that page never touched a wire.
On some of those lines you're paying for power. On the rest, you're paying for paperwork.
And it was never your thermostat. Nobody ever sat at a table with you and read this page out loud.
That's the whole trick. That's all it ever was. My grandmother Ruth kept a household ledger from 1929 to 1939.
It's on the table in front of me right now. April 1934.
The power bill. One line. A number of kilowatt hours, a rate, a total.
That's the whole thing. If a second number had ever shown up on that page, she'd have put her coat on, walked down to the office,
and asked a man what it was for. And she'd have taken me with her so I'd learn how it's done.
She wasn't smarter than you. She just got a bill she could read.
So today we read yours. Fourteen charges. And I'll be straight with you first, because I won't promise you something that isn't true.
Six of these you can kill outright. Five you can shrink.
Three you're stuck with, and no phone call on earth will move them.
And here's what costs people the most money. The three you're stuck with are the three everybody spends the whole call arguing about.
So we're going to sort them, and you'll spend your energy in the right place.
We count down from 14. Everyone comes with the why, because in this house, we don't fight a bill we don't understand.
Number one is the biggest by a long way. In one state, this past April, it cost nine companies $50 million in refunds to 278,000
households. Stay with me for that one. Number 14.
The paper bill fee. Kill it. One to three dollars a month for the crime of receiving a piece of paper.
Look for paper statement, billing fee, or convenience charge.
If it's there, switch to email billing and it's gone tonight.
90 seconds online. $36 a year.
That's not life-changing money, and I know it. I put it at 14 on purpose, so you'd see how small they're willing to go.
If a company will charge you $2 for an envelope, ask yourself what else is sitting on that page.
Number 13. The smart meter opt-out fee.
Kill it. Five to $15 a month, plus a setup charge, for a decision you might have made once, years ago,
and never thought about since. When the smart meters came around, a lot of people opted out.
